newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav Jews say war reparations priority.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav Jews say war reparations priority.

text.p: Yugoslavia's small Jewish community said on Tuesday it doubted the lists of dormant Holocaust-era bank accounts to be revealed by Swiss banks would be complete.
It also said the unresolved issue of German war reparations to eastern European Jews was far more important.
"A big fuss is being made over these accounts now," Aca Singer, president of the Association of Yugoslav Jewish Communities, told Reuters.

"But the human casualties and sufferings are greater and it would be a much better and bigger thing to give some compensation to the few remaining survivors of the Holocaust," he said in an interview.
Swiss banks in July unveiled a list of more than 1,870 pre-1945 foreign account holders who may have been among the six million Jews who perished during the World War Two Holocaust.
The list is believed to include several dozen account holders from ex-Yugoslav states -- Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia, Croatia and Slovenia.
Swiss bankers said the total amount found in the accounts was around 60 million Swiss francs, but an additional list of some 20,000 names was to be published in September.
"I am very sceptical that the list is complete as we already have two concrete cases which we intend to raise with the competent authorities," Singer said.
On Thursday, a U.S. court began hearings on whether Swiss banks could be liable to face class-action suits from Holocaust victims who said the banks stole their assets.
The latest criticism of Switzerland's wartime role has been led by international Jewish organisations and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato.
Singer, himself a former banker, said his search for the account of a granddaughter of a Holocaust victim who had all the details failed since the bank no longer exists.
"I have looked at the list carefully and her grandfather's name is not on it. Many banks no longer exist or have fused or merged and many accounts will be difficult or impossible to trace," he said.
Swiss banks did pay out something earlier but most required death certificates at the time, Singer said.
"In Auschwitz we did not get death certificates. More than 60 members of my own family died there," said Singer, who had spent time in the camp at the age of 18.

"I don't believe there are actual survivors who had accounts simply by biological arithmetic. It is very hard to establish the heirs, especially from Yugoslavia, because 85 percent of Jews from present day Yugoslavia perished."
Germany provided compensation to Jews who suffered during the Holocaust and to concentration camp inmates, but only in Israel and in the West, Singer said.
"Jews from East European countries, including Yugoslavia, did not get a single Deutschemark," he added.
Of around 33,500 Jews in Serbia and Montenegro, some 28,800 died in World War Two.
The Jewish community in Yugoslavia today numbers 3,500 people, compared to the 83,000 on the territory of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1941 before the outbreak of the war.
More than 67,000 Yugoslav Jews perished during the war.
"Of the 15,000 or so survivors, most emigrated while some of those who stayed stopped declaring themselves as Jews," Singer said.
He said the question of war reparations was opened a long time ago but not much had been done.
"We initiated this question but by the time something is done it will be too late, there will be no survivors left."
